standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.5.1, the sentence before Theorem 3.5.6 (mean of the cluster averages), corrected; with Theorems 3.5.3, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 and 3.5.6 for the cluster sample mean
canonical_claim.location: Sentence: p. 138 (PDF p. 156). Definitions 3.5.1, 3.5.2: p. 136 (PDF p. 154). Theorems 3.5.3–3.5.5: p. 137 (PDF p. 155). Theorem 3.5.6: p. 138 (PDF p. 156)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed sentence, p. 138] Alternatively, we can think about the estimator as the average of i.i.d. random variables, with mean $\mathrm{E}[X]$ and common variance $\mathrm{V}[W]$. [Corrected sentence] Alternatively, we can think about the estimator as the average of i.i.d. random variables, with mean $\mathrm{E}[W]$ and common variance $\mathrm{V}[W]$. [Theorems the sentence summarizes, as printed] Theorem 3.5.3. The Cluster Sample Mean Is the Sample Mean of Cluster Averages. Let $(X_{11}, X_{12}, ...X_{1m})$, $(X_{21}, X_{22}, ...X_{2m})$, ..., $(X_{l1}, X_{l2}, ...X_{lm})$ be i.i.d. random vectors, and let $W_i$ be the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ cluster average, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., l\}$. Then $\overline{X} = \overline{W}$. Theorem 3.5.4. The Cluster Sample Mean Is Unbiased for the Population Mean Cluster Average. [Same hypotheses.] Then $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mathrm{E}[W]$. Theorem 3.5.5. Sampling Variance of the Cluster Sample Mean. [Same hypotheses.] Then the sampling variance of the cluster sample mean is $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{j'=1}^{m}\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}]$. Theorem 3.5.6. WLLN for Cluster Samples. Let $(X_{11}, X_{12}, ...X_{1m})$, $(X_{21}, X_{22}, ...X_{2m})$, ..., $(X_{l1}, X_{l2}, ...X_{lm})$ be i.i.d. random vectors with finite $\mathrm{E}[X_{ij}]$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X_{ij}] > 0$, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., l\}$ and $\forall j \in \{1, 2, ..., m\}$, and let $W_i$ be the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ cluster average, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., l\}$. Then $\overline{X} \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{E}[W]$. [Formal content of the corrected sentence] $W_1, W_2, ..., W_l$ are i.i.d. with mean $\mathrm{E}[W] = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{E}[X_{ij}]$ and variance $\mathrm{V}[W]$; $\overline{X} = \overline{W} = \frac{1}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{l} W_i$; $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mathrm{E}[W]$; $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\mathrm{V}[W]}{l}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [p. 135 (PDF p. 153)] To codify this idea, let us now assume that we have $l$ i.i.d. clusters of observations, each consisting of $m$ values and represented by a random vector $(X_{i1}, X_{i2}, ...X_{im})$. Throughout all our discussions of clustering in this book, we will be making the simplifying assumption that all clusters are of an identical size $m$. ... While observations must be independent across clusters (for example, $X_{ij} \perp\!\!\!\perp X_{i'j'}$), within clusters they may be statistically dependent. [p. 136 (PDF p. 154)] Let $n = lm$, so that the number of observations is the number of clusters times the number of observations per cluster. [Definition 3.5.1, p. 136] For i.i.d. random vectors $(X_{11}, X_{12}, ...X_{1m})$, $(X_{21}, X_{22}, ...X_{2m})$, ..., $(X_{l1}, X_{l2}, ...X_{lm})$, the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ cluster average is $W_i = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij}$, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., l\}$. [Footnote 44] Random vectors are i.i.d. if each has the same joint distribution and they satisfy a vector version of mutual independence. [Definition 3.5.2, p. 136] the cluster sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Theorems 3.5.3, 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 are exact for each $l, m \ge 1$: $\overline{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij} = \frac{1}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij} = \overline{W}$; $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \mathrm{V}[\overline{W}] = \frac{\mathrm{V}[W]}{l} = \frac{1}{lm^2}\mathrm{V}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij}\right] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{j'=1}^{m}\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}]$ (Theorems 3.2.4 and 2.3.2). Theorem 3.5.6 is the limit as $l \to \infty$ with $m$ fixed, by Theorem 3.2.8 applied to $W_1, ..., W_l$ (footnote 45 treats $\mathrm{V}[W] = 0$).
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): $\mathrm{E}[X]$ is printed for $\mathrm{E}[W]$; no common coordinate distribution $X$ is assumed in the cluster model, and the theorems on either side use $\mathrm{E}[W]$. The target also carries the exact part of headline claim P001-ch03-H10 (the cluster sample mean equals the mean of cluster averages, is unbiased for $\mathrm{E}[W]$ and has the stated sampling variance), which held up; Theorem 3.5.7 (the CLT for cluster samples, p. 139) is not transcribed here.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 3.5.8 (Consequences of Clustering for the Sample Mean), the common-correlation condition, corrected to pairs $j \ne j'$; and step 1 of the block bootstrap, corrected to $l$ clusters
canonical_claim.location: Example 3.5.8: pp. 140–141 (PDF pp. 158–159). Block bootstrap steps: p. 141 (PDF p. 159). Theorem 3.5.5: p. 137 (PDF p. 155)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement, p. 140] Suppose that: $\forall i, j$, $\mathrm{V}[X_{ij}] = \sigma^2$. $\forall i, j, j'$, $\rho[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}] = \rho > 0$. In other words, the variance of each observation is identical, and every unit within a cluster shares the same correlation. Then, $\forall i, j, j'$, $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}] = \rho[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}]\sigma[X_{ij}]\sigma[X_{ij'}] = \rho\sigma^2$, so $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{j'=1}^{m}\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\left(m\sigma^2 + m(m - 1)\rho\sigma^2\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm}\left(1 + \rho(m - 1)\right)$. [...] Suppose $\rho = 0$; that is, there is no intraclass correlation. Then $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$. [p. 141] Now suppose $\rho = 1$; that is, there is perfect intraclass correlation. Then $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm}(1 + m - 1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm}m = \frac{\sigma^2}{l}$. [Corrected statement] Suppose that: $\forall i, j$, $\mathrm{V}[X_{ij}] = \sigma^2$. $\forall i$ and $\forall j \ne j'$, $\rho[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}] = \rho$ [with $0 \le \rho \le 1$, so that the two extreme cases considered next are covered]. Then, $\forall i$ and $\forall j \ne j'$, $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}] = \rho[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}]\sigma[X_{ij}]\sigma[X_{ij'}] = \rho\sigma^2$, and $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij}] = \sigma^2$, so $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\left(m\sigma^2 + m(m - 1)\rho\sigma^2\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm}\left(1 + \rho(m - 1)\right)$; for $\rho = 0$, $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{lm} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$; for $\rho = 1$, $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{l}$. [Printed block bootstrap, p. 141] 1. Take a with replacement sample of $m$ clusters from our sample, keeping clusters intact. 2. Calculate our would-be estimate using this collected $n$ observations in our block bootstrap sample. 3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 many times. 4. Using the resulting collection of block bootstrap estimates, calculate the standard deviation of the block bootstrap distribution of our estimator. [Corrected step 1] 1. Take a with replacement sample of $l$ clusters from our sample, keeping clusters intact. (A resample of $l$ clusters of size $m$ has $lm = n$ observations, as step 2 and the next paragraph, 'taking with-replacement samples of $l$ clusters from our sample', require.)

[Cluster setting, pp. 135–136 (PDF pp. 153–154)] $l$ i.i.d. clusters, each a random vector $(X_{i1}, X_{i2}, ...X_{im})$ of $m$ values; $n = lm$; cluster sample mean $\overline{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\sum_{j=1}^{m} X_{ij}$ (Definition 3.5.2). [Theorem 3.5.5, p. 137] $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{1}{lm^2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{j'=1}^{m}\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij'}]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$ for $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation; confirmed in part): as printed, the condition includes $j = j'$, where $\rho[X_{ij}, X_{ij}] = 1$ and $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{ij}, X_{ij}] = \sigma^2$, so it would force $\rho = 1$; the calculation that follows treats the $m$ diagonal terms separately and is correct. The validator did not count the passage from '$\rho > 0$' to the case $\rho = 0$ as a separate error (the text introduces it as a new extreme case); stating $0 \le \rho \le 1$ is offered as optional. The design-effect formula $\frac{\sigma^2}{lm}(1 + \rho(m - 1))$ is part of headline claim P001-ch03-H10. Step 1 of the block bootstrap is a procedure, with no statement to prove beyond the count $lm = n$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 4.1.4 (OLS Solution in Matrix Algebra), with the last row of the stacked residual system in its proof corrected ($Y_n$ for $Y_3$); and Theorem 4.1.5 (Properties of Residuals from the OLS Regression Estimator)
canonical_claim.location: Theorem 4.1.4 and the stacked system: p. 148 (PDF p. 166); rest of the proof and Theorem 4.1.5: p. 149 (PDF p. 167); proof of 4.1.5: p. 150 (PDF p. 168). Definition 4.1.2: pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165). Definition 4.1.3: p. 148
canonical_claim.statement: [Theorem 4.1.4, p. 148, as printed; unchanged] OLS Solution in Matrix Algebra. Let $(\mathbf{X}_1, Y_1), (\mathbf{X}_2, Y_2), ..., (\mathbf{X}_n, Y_n)$ be i.i.d. random vectors. Then, if $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ is invertible, the OLS coefficient estimator is given by $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y}$. [Printed proof step, p. 148] For any $(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and for every observation $i$, we can define the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ residual as $e_i = Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})$. We can 'stack' all $n$ of these $e_i$s to form a system of equations, $e_1 = Y_1 - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]1} + b_2X_{[2]1} + ...b_KX_{[K]1})$, $e_2 = Y_2 - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]2} + b_2X_{[2]2} + ...b_KX_{[K]2})$, $\vdots$, $e_n = Y_3 - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]n} + b_2X_{[2]n} + ...b_KX_{[K]n})$. This system of equations can be rewritten in matrix form as ... or equivalently, $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{X}\mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{e} = (e_1, e_2, ..., e_n)^T$, $\mathbf{Y} = (Y_1, Y_2, ..., Y_n)^T$, $\mathbf{b} = (b_0, b_1, b_2, ..., b_K)^T$, and $\mathbb{X}$ is the regressor matrix. [Corrected last row] $e_n = Y_n - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]n} + b_2X_{[2]n} + ... + b_KX_{[K]n})$. [Rest of the proof, p. 149, as printed] Thus, finding the OLS regression estimator is equivalent to the following minimization problem: $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}(\mathbf{e}^T\mathbf{e}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{X}\mathbf{b})^T(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{X}\mathbf{b})$. The first-order condition yields $-2\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{0}$. Solving for $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$: $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y}$. [Theorem 4.1.5, p. 149, as printed] Properties of Residuals from the OLS Regression Estimator. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. random vectors. Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ be the OLS coefficient estimator, and let the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ residual $e_i = Y_i - (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]i} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]i} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]i})$, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$. Then - $\overline{e} = 0$, where $\overline{e} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i$. - $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $\overline{eX_{[k]}} = 0$, where $\overline{eX_{[k]}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_iX_{[k]i}$. - $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $\overline{eX_{[k]}} - \overline{e}\,\overline{X_{[k]}} = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147, with the plus signs before the last terms supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148] the regressor matrix for the OLS regression estimator is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix $\mathbb{X}$ whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. [p. 149 (PDF p. 167)] Note that the condition that $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ must be invertible implies that all the explanatory variables cannot be written as linear combinations of one another; that is, they are not exactly multicollinear. ... In practice, this condition suffices to make the OLS solution unique.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): $Y_3$ is printed for $Y_n$ in one stacked row; the matrix equation directly below is correct. (The missing plus signs before the last terms in this system and in Definition 4.1.2 are a separate typographical finding, P001-C04-N002.) The target also carries headline claim P001-ch04-H2 (the closed-form OLS solution and the residual properties), which held up. Both theorems are exact algebraic statements for each realized sample: for real data $(y_i, x_{[1]i}, ..., x_{[K]i})_{i=1}^{n}$ with $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ invertible, the sum of squared residuals has the unique minimizer $(\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{y}$, and $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$. The book omits the second-order conditions (footnote 4). Theorem 4.1.5 inherits the invertibility of $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The standard error estimator for an OLS coefficient as the square root of a diagonal element of the estimated covariance matrix: the ordinal, corrected (robust, p. 153; classical, p. 155)
canonical_claim.location: p. 153 (PDF p. 171), paragraph after Definition 4.2.1; p. 155 (PDF p. 173), sentence after Definition 4.2.3
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed sentences] [p. 153] Importantly, with the robust sampling variance estimator in hand, we can derive the robust standard error for each OLS regression coefficient: the robust standard error estimator for $\boldsymbol\beta_k$ is the square root of the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ diagonal element of $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$. [p. 155] The classical standard error estimator for $\beta_k$ is then just defined as square root of the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ diagonal element of $\hat{\mathrm{V}}_C[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$. [Corrected sentences] The robust standard error estimator for $\hat\beta_k$ is the square root of the $(k + 1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ diagonal element of $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$ (for $k = 0, ..., K$). The classical standard error estimator for $\hat\beta_k$ is the square root of the $(k + 1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ diagonal element of $\hat{\mathrm{V}}_C[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$ (for $k = 0, ..., K$). [Definitions the sentences refer to, as printed] Definition 4.2.1. Robust Sampling Variance Estimator for OLS. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. random vectors, where $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$. Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ be the OLS coefficient estimator and $e_i = Y_i - (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]i} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]i} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]i})$, $\forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$. Then the robust sampling variance estimator for $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}] = \frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i\right)\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i\right)^{-1} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathrm{diag}(e_1^2, e_2^2, ..., e_n^2)\mathbb{X}(\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}$, where $\mathrm{diag}(e_1^2, e_2^2, ..., e_n^2)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ diagonal element is $e_i^2$ and whose off-diagonal elements are all zero. Definition 4.2.3. Classical Sampling Variance Estimator for OLS. [Same setting.] Then the classical sampling variance estimator for $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is $\hat{\mathrm{V}}_C[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}] = \frac{1}{n}\hat\sigma^2\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i\right)^{-1} = \hat\sigma^2(\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}$, where $\hat\sigma^2 = \hat{\mathrm{V}}[Y - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$. [Formal content] With $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K)$ indexed from 0 and the $(K + 1) \times (K + 1)$ matrices $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$ and $\hat{\mathrm{V}}_C[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]$ with rows and columns numbered from 1, the estimated variance of $\hat\beta_k$ is the entry in row $k + 1$ and column $k + 1$. The two expressions in each definition are equal: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i = \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ and $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}_i = \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{X}^T\mathrm{diag}(e_1^2, ..., e_n^2)\mathbb{X}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [p. 152 (PDF p. 170)] For each coefficient $\beta_k$, it is possible to derive an estimate of the standard error of $\hat\beta_k$: $\hat\sigma[\hat\beta_k] = \sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\beta_k]}$. [Definition 3.2.20, p. 107 (PDF p. 125)] $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\cdot]$ applied to a sample is the unbiased sample variance, $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[X] = \frac{n}{n - 1}(\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2)$. [Footnote 8, p. 155 (PDF p. 173)] The only difference [from the sampling variance estimator given in most textbooks] is that, in most textbooks, $\hat\sigma^2$ uses a denominator of $n - (K + 1)$ instead of $n - 1$. Here $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, X_{[1]i}, ..., X_{[K]i})$ is a row vector, the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row of $\mathbb{X}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation; confirmed in part): an off-by-one ordinal (the coefficients are numbered from 0, so $\beta_k$ sits in position $k + 1$) and a bold $\boldsymbol\beta_k$ for a scalar on p. 153. The validator did not count the missing hat in 'standard error estimator for $\beta_k$' as an error by itself. This is a correction to a definitional sentence; the provable content is the equality of the two forms of each estimator.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.2.3, the display reducing the asymptotic covariance of the OLS estimator under a linear CEF and homoskedasticity, with the stray observation subscript removed
canonical_claim.location: p. 155 (PDF p. 173), display beginning $n\mathrm{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}] \approx$; the sandwich form: p. 152 (PDF p. 170)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Suppose we assume that $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon|X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}] = 0$ and $\mathrm{V}[\varepsilon|X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}] = \sigma^2$ for all possible values of $X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}$. The first assumption is equivalent to linearity of $\mathrm{E}[Y|X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}]$, and the second assumption is known as (conditional) homoskedasticity. Again, let $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$. Then, as before, $n\mathrm{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}] \approx \left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}_i^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1} = \left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}\left(\sigma^2\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1} = \sigma^2\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}$, where the approximation follows from Section 4.2.2, and the first equality follows from the facts that $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}] = \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}|\mathbf{X}]]$ (by the Law of Iterated Expectations) and $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2|\mathbf{X}] = \sigma^2$ (by the linearity and homoskedasticity assumptions). [Corrected first line] $n\mathrm{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}] \approx \left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}$. [Formal content] Let $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]})$ be a random row vector with $\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]$ finite and invertible, and let $\varepsilon$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon|\mathbf{X}] = 0$ and $\mathrm{V}[\varepsilon|\mathbf{X}] = \sigma^2$. Then $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2|\mathbf{X}] = \sigma^2$, $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}] = \sigma^2\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]$, and $\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1} = \sigma^2\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Section 4.2.2, p. 152] Define the vector of errors $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ as the differences between the observed values of $Y$ and the (true) BLP of $Y$ given the observed values of $X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}$: $\boldsymbol\varepsilon = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{X}\boldsymbol\beta$. We can then decompose $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T(\mathbb{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \boldsymbol\beta + (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. Under the usual plug-in regularity conditions, $\sqrt{n}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \boldsymbol\beta)$ converges in distribution to a multivariate normal random vector with expectation zero and covariance matrix $\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\left(\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}]\right)^{-1}$, where $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$ (p. 153).
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): a stray observation subscript $i$ in the last factor of the first line; the following lines show the intended matrix. The formal content is the exact matrix identity behind the two equalities of the display; the '$\approx$' (the asymptotic covariance of $\sqrt{n}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \boldsymbol\beta)$) is stated in the book without proof. Part of headline claim P001-ch04-H4 (classical standard errors as the plug-in estimator under a linear CEF and homoskedasticity).
